CausalChain: Low-dose radiotherapy -> Induction of immunogenic cell death and nanoparticle-enhanced ICD -> Release of neoantigens and inflammatory cytokines (e.g., IFN-γ) -> Expansion of circulating precursor exhausted CD8⁺ T cells in the STIE (tracked via advanced omics profiling) -> Increased recruitment of these T cells into the TIME (aided by nanoparticle carriers) -> PD-1 blockade lifts inhibitory signals -> Differentiation into effective cytotoxic T cells -> Enhanced antitumor response
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that a precisely timed, multi-modal therapeutic strategy—combining low-dose, fractionated radiotherapy with nanoparticle-facilitated enhancement of immunogenic cell death and real-time immune profiling, followed by PD-1 inhibitor therapy—will synergistically convert immunologically ‘cold’ tumors into ‘hot’ tumors. This sequential approach is expected to selectively expand precursor exhausted CD8⁺ T cells in the systemic immune environment (STIE), promote their effective recruitment to the tumor microenvironment (TIME), and, by lifting PD-1 mediated inhibitory signals during a defined optimal window, drive their differentiation into potent cytotoxic T cells, thereby significantly improving antitumor efficacy.
Abstract: In this study, we propose a refined sequential therapy for solid tumors, such as non‐small cell lung cancer, which integrates low‐dose, fractionated radiotherapy with advanced immune monitoring and nanoparticle‐mediated immunogenic enhancement, followed by precisely timed PD-1 inhibitor administration. The proposed regimen aims to transiently expand precursor exhausted CD8⁺ T cells by initially inducing immunogenic cell death and a surge of neoantigens and inflammatory cytokines. This is further augmented by nanoparticle-delivered agents that promote immunogenic cell death while mitigating T cell exhaustion. Continuous real-time single-cell transcriptomic and digital biomarker profiling defines the optimal window for subsequent PD-1 blockade, thereby effectively converting “cold” tumors into “hot” tumors with a robust antitumor response.
Orignal_vs_New: The original hypothesis advocated a sequential regimen of low-dose, fractionated radiotherapy followed by PD-1 inhibition to expand precursor exhausted CD8⁺ T cells and convert cold tumors into hot ones. The revised hypothesis builds on this causal chain by explicitly incorporating nanoparticle-mediated enhancement of immunogenic cell death and state-of-the-art real-time immune monitoring (e.g., single-cell RNA sequencing and digital biomarkers) to address previous gaps regarding dosing, timing, and mechanistic clarity. Each step of the original causal reasoning—from radiotherapy-induced ICD and neoantigen release, precursor T cell expansion, recruitment into the tumor microenvironment, to the final differentiation upon PD-1 blockade—is preserved and enhanced by leveraging contemporary technological capabilities, thereby increasing the feasibility and translational potential of the approach.
